en: The *Mahāsāṃghika Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, translated by the Śramaṇa Faxian of Pingyang together with Buddhabhadra during the Eastern Jin dynasty:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Of the winter month, one night has passed and only one night remains."
Three months remain.
Old age and death have drawn near, and the Buddha-dharma is about to perish.
Venerable friends!
For the sake of attaining the Way, one should practice with single-minded diligence and vigor. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas, through single-minded diligence and vigor, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"How much more so for the other factors conducive to enlightenment!
"Those who have not yet received full ordination have already departed.
"The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall we do first?"
One person should respond:
"The *poṣadha* and recitation of the precepts. "Venerable sirs!"
The bhikṣuṇīs who have not arrived shall announce their *chanda* and purification.
With palms joined like ten fingernails, I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas;
now that I am about to recite the precepts, the Saṃgha should listen with a single mind.
Even regarding minor offenses, one’s mind should feel great dread;
having committed a transgression, repent with single-mindedness, and never commit it again.
The horse of the mind gallops toward evil paths; when abandoned to heedlessness, it is difficult to restrain.
The Buddha has taught all the precepts and practices, Just like sharp reins and bits.
When the Buddha’s mouth proclaims the instructions, The virtuous are able to believe and accept them;
Such a person is a well-trained horse, Able to shatter the army of afflictions.
If one does not accept instruction, nor takes delight in the precepts,
this person’s horse is untamed and they are submerged in the army of afflictions.
If a person guards the precepts as a gayal ox loves its tail;
Binding the mind with heedfulness, like a monkey bound by chains,
one exerts diligent effort day and night for the sake of seeking true wisdom;
such a person, within the Buddha’s Dharma, is able to attain a pure livelihood.
"Venerable sirs, may the Saṃgha listen!
Today is the fifteenth day for the *poṣadha* and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha with one mind perform the *poṣadha* together by reciting the *Prātimokṣa*."
[The announcement] is thus made. "Venerable sirs!

Now we shall perform the Poṣadha together and recite the Prātimokṣa. May the Saṃgha listen with one mind. Those who have committed an offense should confess it; those without offense should remain silent."

Because of their silence, it should be known that the noble ladies (āryā) are pure; as with the question and answer for each individual bhikṣuṇī, so too is it for the three proclamations made within this assembly of bhikṣuṇīs.

If a bhikṣuṇī, when the second and third proclamations have been made within such a community of bhikṣuṇīs, remembers having committed an offense but does not disclose it, she incurs the offense of intentional lying.
Venerable sisters! The Buddha has declared that the offense of intentional lying is a dharma that obstructs the path.

If a bhikṣuṇī seeks purity within this matter, she should acknowledge any offense she remembers; by acknowledging it, she will find peace, but by failing to acknowledge it, her offense becomes deeper.
Venerable sirs!
The introduction to the Prātimokṣa has been recited.
Now I ask the venerable sirs: [Is it pure?]
"Is it pure in this regard?
He asks thus a second and a third time:
"Venerable sirs!"
"In this matter, you are pure, for you remain silent;
thus it shall be held as such. "Venerable sirs!
These eight *pārājika* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*."

"If a bhikṣuṇī has received full ordination within a harmonious assembly of both orders of the Saṃgha, and she does not relinquish her precepts, nor does she emerge from the weakness of her vows, yet engages in sexual intercourse—even with an animal—this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, in a village or in an open space, takes what is not given by means of theft, and a king or his officials seize her, kill her, bind her, or banish her, saying:
'Hey, woman!'"
“You thief! You fool!
If a bhikṣuṇī thus takes what is not given, she commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community.
“If a bhikṣuṇī, with her own hand, deprives a person of life; or seeks out and provides a knife to a killer; or instructs another to die, or praises death:”
"Alas! What is the use of living such a wretched life?
Death is better than life."
Forming such an intention and conceiving such a thought, she uses skillful means to praise the joy of death, so that she dies for this reason and no other.
This bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense; she should not dwell together [with the Saṃgha].
"If a bhikṣuṇī, not knowing and not having understood, claims for herself that she has attained a superhuman state, a noble knowledge and vision of excellence, saying:
'I know thus; I see thus.'"
Later, whether he has been investigated or not, having committed an offense and desiring to seek purification, he speaks thus:
"Venerable One!..."
‘I claim to know what I do not know and to see what I have not seen; my words are empty, deceptive, and untrue.
Except in the case of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), such a bhikṣuṇī commits a *pārājika* offense and should not live in community with the others.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, allows a man who has a lustful mind to touch her from below the shoulder to above the knee and experiences pleasure thereby, this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense; she should not live in community."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, with lustful intent, speaks with a man who has lustful intent when he extends his hand into her reach; or receives his grasping of her hand, or his grasping of her robe; or comes to invite her joyfully to sit, or bends her body toward him, or makes an appointment to go away together—this bhikṣuṇī is defeated (pārājika) and should not live in communion."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, does not disclose it to others, and after that bhikṣu has departed from his dwelling, died, or left the religious life, she later says:
'I previously knew that this bhikṣu had committed a grave offense.'"
If she does not speak of it to others and does not wish for others to know, that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in community with the others.

"If a bhikṣuṇī knows that the Saṃgha, being in harmony, has performed a formal act of censure (karma) against a bhikṣu in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, yet she complies with him before such a formal act has been lawfully carried out."
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Āryā!

This bhikṣu has been subjected to the formal act of suspension (utkṣepaṇa-karman) by the harmonious Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya; do not comply with him as long as he has not acted in accordance with the Dharma."
When these bhikṣuṇīs were being admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs, they spoke thus:
"We will not comply; who indeed would comply?
When the bhikṣuṇīs admonished them a second and a third time in this manner, they should abandon such behavior; if they do so, it is well.
"If she does not relinquish it, this bhikṣuṇī is defeated (pārājika) and should not live in community with the others. "Venerable ladies!
The eight pārājika rules have been recited; if a bhikṣuṇī commits any one of these rules, that bhikṣuṇī should not live in community with the others."
As it was before, so it is after.
A bhikṣuṇī who has committed a pārājika offense should not live in community with the others.
Now I ask the noble ladies: Are you pure in this matter?
A second and third time he asked in the same manner:
"Venerable sirs! Since you are silent, you are pure in this matter; let it be so held."
“Venerable ladies! These nineteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*.

If a bhikṣuṇī acts as a messenger to bring about the union of a man and a woman—whether for taking a wife or for illicit intercourse—even for a mere moment, this rule constitutes an initial offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, resentment, or displeasure, slanders a pure and innocent bhikṣuṇī with a groundless charge of a pārājika offense, desiring to destroy that bhikṣuṇī’s pure conduct."
At a later time, whether he is investigated or not, he speaks thus:
"This matter was baseless; I spoke these words because I was dwelling in malice and resentment."
This is an offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for the first time.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and resentment, because she is displeased, should defame a bhikṣuṇī who is not guilty of a *pārājika* offense by charging her with a *pārājika* offense based on a minor matter belonging to a different category, desiring to destroy that person's holy life (*brahmacarya*)."

If, at a later time, whether she has been investigated or not, she—out of a state of resentment—accuses that bhikṣuṇī with a minor matter belonging to a different category, this constitutes an offense of the first degree, a saṃghāvaśeṣa.

"If a bhikṣuṇī engages in quarreling or mutual verbal abuse—whether with a layperson or one who has left the household—for even a brief moment during the day, or even fights and exchanges words with a park-attendant or a śrāmaṇera, this is an offense of the first category, a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"If a bhikṣuṇī travels without a companion bhikṣuṇī, she must not go beyond the boundary of a village, except at other times.
'Other times' refers to when one is ill or does not wish [to travel]; these are called 'other times.'"
This is an offense of the Saṃghāvaśeṣa class, involving an initial transgression.
"If a bhikṣuṇī stays overnight apart from other bhikṣuṇīs, except at the appropriate times.
The 'appropriate times' are: when one is ill, or when a city is besieged by bandits or in a state of turmoil; these are called the appropriate times."
This is an offense of the first category, a saṃghāvaśeṣa:
"If a bhikṣuṇī ordains someone whose guardian has not given permission, this is an offense of the first category, a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another woman has committed an offense and that her relatives wish to punish her, should ordain her—except at other times.
'Other times' refers to when she was previously ordained by non-Buddhists; this is called 'other times.'"
This is an offense of the first category, a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
"If a bhikṣuṇī crosses a river alone at a ferry crossing, this is an offense of the first category, a saṃghāvaśeṣa."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a bhikṣuṇī saṃgha has performed a formal act of censure (ukkhepanīyakamma) in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya, yet before the procedure has been rendered legal, she herself grants the relinquishment of that act without first informing the saṃgha."
This rule constitutes an initial offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

The ten matters are concluded. "If a bhikṣuṇī, whether with a mind free from desire or with a mind of desire, takes robes, bowls, food, drink, or medicinal decoctions for illness from a man, this rule constitutes an initial offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
'You may accept this gift from this man; what does it matter to you whether he has lustful thoughts or not?'"
"However, you must not let your mind stray; once you have accepted the gift, you may use it according to the circumstances.
The bhikṣuṇīs should then admonish that bhikṣuṇī:
"Do not speak such words:"
"You should accept this offering; what concern is it whether a man's mind is defiled or undefiled?
Provided that you yourself remain undefiled in mind, you may accept the gift and use it according to the circumstances."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, desiring to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, persists in matters that lead to a schism and engages in dispute over them, she should be admonished thus a second and third time; it would be well if she were to relinquish this matter.
If she does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
||| "If a bhikṣuṇī, for the purpose of breaking up a harmonious Saṃgha, takes up matters that cause a schism and disputes over them..."
The bhikṣuṇīs should say to this bhikṣuṇī: "Venerable lady!
Do not strive to break the harmony of the Saṃgha by persistently maintaining the causes for schism and engaging in dispute; you should act in concert with the Saṃgha."

"Why is this? Because when the Saṃgha is harmonious, joyful, and without dispute, practicing together under a single training as if water and milk were mixed, and dwelling in peace according to the Dharma as they speak it.
If that bhikṣuṇī, when admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs, persists and does not relinquish her position, she should be admonished a second and a third time; if she relinquishes it, that is well.
If she does not relinquish it, then after up to three admonitions, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If various bhikṣuṇīs, with like-minded intent, assist one another—whether one, two, or many—and speak with the same words and hold the same views, desiring to break the harmony of the Saṃgha..."
When these bhikṣuṇīs are being admonished by other bhikṣuṇīs, those bhikṣuṇīs who side with them say:
"Venerable ladies!
Do not speak of this bhikṣuṇī's good or bad qualities."
Why is this? Because these bhikṣuṇīs speak according to the Dharma and speak according to the Vinaya.
Whatever these bhikṣuṇīs have said is exactly what we desire.
"Whatever matter this bhikṣuṇī has seen and approved, we also approve.
This bhikṣuṇī speaks with knowledge, not without knowledge.
The other bhikṣuṇīs should then admonish those bhikṣuṇīs who agree with her:
“Venerable lady!
Do not speak these words:
‘The bhikṣuṇī speaks according to the Dharma; the bhikṣuṇī speaks according to the Vinaya.’”
Why is that? Because these are bhikṣuṇīs who speak what is not in accordance with the Dharma, not bhikṣuṇīs who speak in accordance with the Vinaya, Noble Lady!
Do not assist in the schism of the Saṃgha; you should instead delight in the harmony of the Saṃgha. Why is this?
When the Saṃgha is harmonious, joyful, and free from dispute, they train together as one, like water mixed with milk, dwelling in peace and happiness according to the Dharma.
If this bhikṣuṇī, when admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs, persists in her refusal to relinquish [the matter], she should be admonished a second and a third time; if she relinquishes it, that is well.
If she does not relinquish this practice even after the third admonition, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, unreasonably slanders the Saṃgha, saying:
'The Saṃgha follows desire, follows hatred, follows fear, and follows delusion; the Saṃgha acts out of desire, hatred, fear, and delusion; for this reason it censures me.'"
The other bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Venerable lady,
do not speak such words."
"The Saṃgha follows craving, follows hatred, follows fear, and follows delusion; the Saṃgha relies upon craving, hatred, fear, and delusion.
Why is this? Because the Saṃgha does not follow craving, hatred, fear, or delusion, you must not harbor anger or slander the Saṃgha unreasonably.

If this bhikṣuṇī, when admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs, persists in her refusal to relinquish [the matter], she should be admonished a second and a third time; it would be well if she relinquishes this matter.
If she does not relinquish it, this rule constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense after the third admonition.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, being obstinate and contrary,
when the other bhikṣuṇīs instruct her in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya regarding the common rules of the community, should follow her own will and say:
'Do not speak to me of what is good or what is bad.'"
"I will not tell you whether it is good or bad.
The bhikṣuṇīs should then admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Āryā!..."
The bhikṣuṇīs shall instruct you together in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya; do not rely on your own words.
You should believe and accept what the bhikṣuṇīs teach you, and you, in turn, should instruct the bhikṣuṇīs in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
Why is this? Because among the disciples of the Tathāgata, they instruct one another and admonish one another, thereby emerging together from their transgressions; thus, wholesome dharmas increase.
If this bhikṣuṇī, when admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs, persists in her refusal to relinquish [the matter], she should be admonished a second and a third time; if she relinquishes it, that is well.
If she does not relinquish this practice even after three admonitions, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If two bhikṣuṇīs live in close association and conceal each other's transgressions, the other bhikṣuṇīs should admonish those bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
'Venerable ladies!'"
"Do not associate with one another by concealing each other's faults; by associating in this way, wholesome dharmas will not arise.
If that bhikṣuṇī, when admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs, persists and does not relinquish this, she should be admonished a second and a third time. If she relinquishes this matter, it is well;
if she does not relinquish this practice even after the third admonition, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, seeing that [other] bhikṣuṇīs are living at a distance, should encourage them by saying:
'You should live in close proximity and conceal each other's faults; do not live apart, for it will not hinder the growth of wholesome dharmas.'"
"Other people also live in close proximity like this, yet the Saṃgha cannot prevent them; it is only because you treat us with contempt that we have forbidden you!
The bhikṣuṇīs should then admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Āryā!..."

"O [Name] and [Name], you should dwell far apart from one another; do not encourage one another to dwell in close proximity or to conceal each other's transgressions. Dwelling in close proximity does not hinder the arising of wholesome dharmas.
Do not speak these words:
'Other people also dwell in close proximity, yet the Sangha cannot prevent them; you are merely being restricted because they look down upon you!'"
"If that bhikṣuṇī, when admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs, persists and does not relinquish [her position], she should be admonished a second and a third time; if she relinquishes it, that is well.
If she does not relinquish it, this matter constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense after the third admonition."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and wishing to abandon the precepts, should speak thus:

'I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṃgha; I renounce the teaching, I renounce communal residence and communal meals; I renounce the sūtras and śāstras, I renounce the śramaṇīs of the Śākya clan—what use have I for these śramaṇīs of the Śākya clan?'"
"There are other superior places where I shall practice the holy life.
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Venerable One!..."
Do not, out of anger, abandon the precepts by saying:
"I renounce the Buddha," up to "I renounce the Śramaṇī of the Śākya clan.
To renounce the Buddha is unwholesome.
"If the bhikṣuṇīs, when thus admonished, still obstinately persist and do not relinquish it, they should be admonished a second and a third time; it would be well if they relinquish this matter.
If they do not relinquish this practice even after being admonished up to three times, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
The nineteen matters are concluded: "Venerable sirs!
The nineteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas have been recited: eleven are offenses upon the first commission, and eight require up to three admonitions."

If a bhikṣuṇī commits any one of these offenses, she must undergo the *mānatva* penance for half a month within both assemblies. Subsequently, when it comes time for the *ābhāṣaṇā*, she should have her offense cleared within an assembly of twenty members from both orders of the Saṃgha, acting in a manner that accords with the minds of the assembly.
If among the twenty persons even one is missing, this bhikṣuṇī is not said to have been cleared of her offense; the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs should reprove her—this is called the proper time.
"Now I ask the Venerable Ones:
Are you pure in this matter?
He asks a second and a third time in the same manner.
"Venerable sirs! Since there is silence, you are pure in this matter;
let it be so held. "Venerable sirs!"
These thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her robes and having relinquished the *kaṭhina* privileges, should obtain an extra robe, she may keep it for up to ten days."
If she exceeds [this limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her robes and having relinquished the *kaṭhina* cloth, should stay apart from any one of her five robes in another place for even one night, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (*saṃgha-karman*), it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her robes and having relinquished the kaṭhina privileges, should obtain an out-of-season robe, she may accept it if she needs it and make it up quickly; if it is insufficient and she has a source from which more can be obtained to complete it, she is permitted to keep it for one month.
If she keeps it longer than that, whether it is sufficient or not, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, with her own hand, takes hold of raw gold or silver, or causes another to take hold of them to lift or process them for the purpose of attachment, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣuṇī engages in various kinds of buying and selling, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī asks for a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, except during the [prescribed] time."

Regarding "other times": the time when one's robes have been lost is called "other times. If a bhikṣuṇī, at such a time, obtains robes by begging from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, she may accept an upper robe and a lower robe if they are offered according to her own wish.
If she accepts it beyond this limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a householder or a householder’s wife prepares the price for a robe for a bhikṣuṇī, saying:
'I have prepared the price for such a robe; buy such a robe and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī.'"
If this bhikṣuṇī, having not been previously invited to do so at her own discretion, goes to encourage [the laywoman] for the sake of obtaining something fine, saying: "Excellent, upāsikā!
Prepare the price for such a robe and buy me a robe of such a color."
If she should obtain the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"For the sake of a bhikṣuṇī, if two laymen or two laywomen each provide the price for a robe, saying:
'We have provided such and such a price for a robe; we shall buy such and such a robe and give it to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so. "
If this bhikṣuṇī, without having been previously invited to do so at her own discretion, approaches a householder for the sake of obtaining fine garments and says:
"Prepare such and such amounts of money for the price of clothing for me individually, and together provide me with a single robe."
If, for the sake of desiring something fine, she should obtain such a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If, on behalf of a bhikṣuṇī, a king or a high minister sends a messenger with the value of a robe to give to that bhikṣuṇī, and the messenger arrives at the bhikṣuṇī’s location and says:
'Noble Lady!'"
"This garment price has been sent by either a king or a high minister. Noble Lady!
You should accept this price for the garment."
That bhikṣuṇī should speak to the messenger as follows:
“It is not in accordance with the rule for bhikṣuṇīs to accept the price of this robe.
When I have need of a robe and obtain a pure robe, I may accept it with my own hands and keep it after having made it into a bhikṣuṇī’s robe.”
The messenger said to the bhikṣuṇī:
"Āryā! Is there an attendant who constantly performs services for the bhikṣuṇīs?"
That bhikṣuṇī should point out a person in charge of affairs— whether a park-keeper or an upāsaka—
and should tell that person upon their arrival:
"Excellent, manager!..."
"Purchase such and such clothing for such and such a price and give it to that certain bhikṣuṇī.
When that bhikṣuṇī needs clothing, she shall come; then you shall give her the clothing."
Having either exhorted him himself or sent someone else to exhort him, the messenger returns to the bhikṣuṇī and says:
"Āryā, I have exhorted the person designated as the steward regarding the making of the robe."
"Noble Lady!
When you need robes, go and take them; we shall give robes to the Noble Lady.
A bhikṣuṇī who needs robes should go to the place of the attendant and request robes, saying these words:
"I need robes! I need robes!
He requested thus a second and a third time.
If one obtains the robe-cloth, it is well.
If not, on the fourth, fifth, and sixth days, one should stand silently before the steward; if one obtains the robe-cloth then, it is well.
If not, to seek it beyond that point and obtain the robe-cloth constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she does not obtain the robe, she should go herself or send a messenger to the place where the price for the robe originated and say:
"The price for a robe was sent by you for a certain bhikṣuṇī; however, that bhikṣuṇī did not ultimately receive it."
"You should know this for yourself and not let it be lost; such is the nature of things.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having begged for bedding and mats, uses them herself for robes, bowls, food, drink, or medicinal decoctions for illness, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when someone gives something to her for one purpose, uses it for another, she commits a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī begs for food and makes use of it for robes, bowls, food, drink, or medicinal decoctions, she commits a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra alms bowl, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī discards her old saṃghāṭī at her place of residence and says,
'Whoever wishes to take it,
let them take it,' and later takes it back, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

"If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally sets aside her saṃghāṭī robe herself or causes another to set it aside, and after five or six days has passed, neither sews it herself nor causes another to sew it, except in the case of illness, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī says to a śikṣamāṇā:
'Give me a robe and I shall grant you full ordination,' yet after taking the robe she does not grant the full ordination, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣuṇī purchases a heavy robe for more than four kārṣāpaṇas, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī purchases a fine, light robe for more than two and a half kārṣāpaṇas, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣuṇī possesses an extra bowl, she may keep it for ten days.
If she exceeds this period, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣuṇī’s bowl has fewer than five mends, yet she begs for a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.”
This bowl should be relinquished within the Saṃgha; it should be given to the lowest-ranking bowl among the community of bhikṣuṇīs. It should be instructed thus:
"You, bhikṣuṇī, shall receive this bowl until it breaks; such is the nature of the Dharma."
“If a bhikṣuṇī is ill, she is permitted to keep for seven days and consume as medicine whatever is required for her ailment: ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, fresh butter, and fat.”
If, after seven days have passed, one wears the robe without relinquishing it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī gives a robe to another bhikṣuṇī, and later, out of anger and displeasure, either takes it back herself or causes someone else to take it back, saying:
'Bhikṣuṇī, give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.'"
If she obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī engages in various kinds of trading involving raw materials or processed goods, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī herself begs for thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a householder or a housewife has a weaver weave a robe for a bhikṣuṇī..."
This bhikṣuṇī, having not been previously invited, went to the weaver and exhorted him, saying:
"Do you know? This robe is being made for me;
weave it well so that it is fine, long, and wide, and I shall give you money, the value of the money, food, and the value of the food."
If a bhikṣuṇī, having exhorted in this manner, receives money or its equivalent, food or its equivalent, and thereby obtains a robe, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, within ten days before the end of the three-month summer retreat, receives an urgent gift of cloth (ātyayika-cīvara), and that bhikṣuṇī requires it, she may take and store it until the time for robes."
If she keeps it beyond the permitted time, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another has purchased something, buys it up [to acquire it for herself], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another's property was intended for the Saṃgha, diverts it to herself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The thirty matters are concluded. "Venerable sisters!..."
The thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas have already been explained.
Now I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this matter?
A second and third time he asked in the same manner:
"Venerable sirs, since you are silent, you are pure in this matter; thus shall it be held."
“Venerable sisters!
These one hundred and forty-one *pāyattika* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*.
‘If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly speaks a falsehood, it is a *pāyattika*.’”
"If a bhikṣuṇī speaks of the physical characteristics of another, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī engages in double-tongued speech, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a dispute has been settled by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, should again raise the matter, saying:
'This formal act (karma) was not properly concluded; it should be performed again.'"
If one acts with such intentional causes and conditions, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī instructs a person who has not received full ordination in the wording of the Dharma, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, before one who has not yet received full ordination, claims for herself a superhuman state, saying:
'I know thus; I see thus,' even if she speaks the truth, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), should speak of it to one who has not received full ordination, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (saṃghakamma), it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Saṃgha is about to distribute goods, first consents to their being given and later objects, saying:
‘Āryā! You have diverted the property of the Saṃgha out of favoritism toward your friends.’”
“[This is] a pāyattika.
‘If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Prātimokṣa Sūtra is being recited during the half-month [observance], should say:
“Noble lady!...”’”
"Why do you speak of these minor precepts?
They cause the bhikṣuṇīs to give rise to doubt and regret.
To thus disparage the precepts through such causes and conditions as these constitutes a pāyattika offense.
The ten matters are concluded: "If a bhikṣuṇī destroys seeds or ruins a 'village of spirits' (a grove), it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī annoys another with discordant speech, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of resentment, reproaches [another], it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, at a monastery dwelling on open ground, spreads out a bed, a chair, a mattress, or a pillow—whether she spreads them herself or causes another to spread them..."
If she does not lift it herself when departing, nor causes another to lift it, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, within a communal dwelling in a covered area, spreads out bedding or causes another to spread it out..."
If she does not herself lift [the bedding] when departing, nor causes another to lift it, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, while inside a monastic dwelling, either drags a bhikṣuṇī out herself or causes another to drag her out, even down to saying:
'Bhikṣuṇī, you must go out.'"
One who speaks these words commits a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has already spread out bedding within a communal dwelling, comes later and spreads her own out with the intent to cause disturbance, saying:
'Those who do not like this should leave of their own accord.'"
If one acts through such causes and conditions, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī spreads out a bed with pointed legs on an upper story of a monastic dwelling and sits or lies upon it, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that water contains living beings, pours it over grass or mud, or causes another to pour it, it is a pāyattika.

"If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally causes another bhikṣuṇī to fall into doubt or regret, even for a moment, such that she finds no joy, and for reasons no different from those previously stated, it is a pāyattika."

The twenty matters are concluded: "If a bhikṣuṇī has been invited to a place where a single meal is provided, a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill should eat only that one meal; should she exceed this, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī eats at various places, except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika.
The 'appropriate times' are: when one is ill, and when robes are being offered; these are called the appropriate times."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having made a formal gift of her robe to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, subsequently uses it without relinquishing the claim, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another has already eaten their fill, encourages them to eat more out of a desire to annoy them—when that person has left their seat without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (refusal of further food)—it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī places in her mouth anything that has not been given and not accepted—except for water and tooth-sticks—it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī eats stored food, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the home of a layperson and is offered cakes or parched grain at will, she may accept two or three bowls and go outside to eat them together with bhikṣuṇīs who are not ill."
If a bhikṣuṇī accepts food and goes outside to eat it alone, without sharing with other bhikṣuṇīs who are not ill, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of playful mirth, hides another’s robe, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case, or causes someone else to hide them, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī eats apart from the community, except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika.
The 'appropriate times' are: when one is ill, when there is work regarding robes, when traveling, when on a boat, when there is a large assembly, and when a meal is offered by non-Buddhists."

The thirty matters are concluded: "If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, for her own sake burns grass, wood, or cow dung—whether she burns it herself or causes another to burn it—except in cases of necessity, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī stays in the same room as a person who has not received full ordination for more than three nights, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having already given her consent (*chanda*) for a formal act (*karmavācanā*), later becomes resentful and displeased, saying:
'I did not give my consent; it was not properly given. This formal act is not valid; I do not give this consent.'"
[Pāyattika. "If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī: 'Āryā!'"
"Let us enter the village together; when we arrive there, I shall give you food—either giving it to you myself or sending someone else to do so.
Later, wishing to drive him away, he then said:
"Go away! I do not find it pleasant to dwell with you; I find it pleasant to dwell alone.
If one acts on this basis without deviation, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī speaks thus: 'Venerable lady!
I know that the World-Honored One has taught that these are dharmas that obstruct the path; yet practicing these dharmas cannot obstruct the path.'"
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her, saying:
"Venerable lady!
Do not slander the Blessed One; to slander the Blessed One is unwholesome."
"The World-Honored One does not speak such words; the World-Honored One declares that the dharmas which obstruct the path truly do obstruct the path.
You must abandon this evil course.
If, when admonished in this manner, he persists and does not abandon it, he should be admonished a second and a third time. If he abandons it, that is well.
If she does not relinquish it, the Saṃgha should perform the formal act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) against that bhikṣuṇī; [if she continues], it is a pāyattika.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has held evil views and has not relinquished them, and that the Saṃgha has performed the formal act of suspension against her in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, yet she—while the formal act has not been performed in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya—eats together with her or dwells in the same room as her, it is a pāyattika."
"If a śrāmaṇerī should say:
'The Tathāgata has said that sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the path; I know that practicing sexual desire cannot obstruct the path.'"
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her, saying:
"You, śrāmaṇerī, must not slander the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One.
The Blessed One did not speak such words; the Blessed One has said that sensual desire is truly an obstacle to the Path."
"You must abandon this evil view.
When he has been thus admonished, if he persists and does not abandon it, he should be admonished a second and a third time; if he abandons it, that is well.
If she does not relinquish it, she should be expelled with these words:
"From this day forward, you, śrāmaṇerikā, must not say:
'The Buddha is my teacher.'"
"Furthermore, you must not stay together with a bhikṣuṇī for more than three nights.
Go away; you are not permitted to dwell here.

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a śrāmaṇerikā has not abandoned her evil views, fails to expel her and instead improperly entices her back, supports her, eats with her, or dwells with her, it is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a new robe, she must apply one of three kinds of discoloration: either blue, black, or madder.
If she uses it without applying one of these three kinds of discoloration, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, whether it be a jewel or what is considered a jewel, takes it herself within a garden or causes another to take it, except at other times, it is a pāyattika."
As for "other times": if a bhikṣuṇī takes, or causes another to take, either actual jewels or things considered jewels, with the thought:
"If the owner comes seeking them, I shall give them back."
This is called "other occasions.
If a bhikṣuṇī terrifies another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
The forty matters are concluded. If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that water contains living organisms, drinks it, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī gives food with her own hand to male or female renunciants of other sects who are without robes, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī sits in a place of sexual intercourse within a household where food is being served, knowing it to be so, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī sits in a secluded place at a house where food is being served, knowing [it to be so], it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī observes an army on the march, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī, having a legitimate reason, stays among an army for three nights;
if she exceeds this, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī, having a legitimate reason, stays among an army for three nights, and if she watches the army set out, the battle standards, or the array of forces, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and resentment, strikes another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and resentment, brandishes her palm as if wielding a blade toward another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī plays in the water, it is a pāyattika.
The fifty matters are concluded. "If a bhikṣuṇī points her finger at another, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that she is with a band of thieves, agrees to travel together with them on the road, even as far as a village, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī digs the earth with her own hand or causes another to dig it, giving instructions, saying:
'Dig this ground.'"

“Pāyattika. ‘If a bhikṣuṇī accepts an individual invitation for four months, she may do so; if she accepts it beyond that period, it is a pāyattika, except in the case of a renewed invitation or a long-term invitation during the *pravāraṇā*.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
'Venerable sister! You should train yourself;
do not commit the five classes of offenses.'"
He replied: "I will not follow your words.
If I see another venerable one who is tranquil, learned, a bearer of the Dharma, and possesses deep understanding, I shall consult him; whatever he says, I shall accept and practice."
"Except at other times, one who speaks thus commits a pāyattika.
A bhikṣu who desires the benefit of the Dharma should train accordingly and should also question other bhikṣuṇīs."
"If a bhikṣuṇī drinks alcohol, for every swallow it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī treats another bhikṣuṇī with contempt, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, while other bhikṣuṇīs are engaged in a dispute, stands by silently listening [with the thought],
'I shall remember what they say,' and acts for this purpose and no other, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Saṃgha intends to settle a matter, does not give her consent (*chanda*) and departs without informing them, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, during the fortnightly recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, should say:
'I have only now learned that this rule is included in the Sūtras and was recited within the fortnightly Prātimokṣa.'"

If the other bhikṣuṇīs know that the bhikṣuṇī in question has previously sat through two or three recitations of the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, let alone more, she is not exempt from fault on account of her ignorance; she shall be dealt with according to the Dharma in accordance with the offense she has committed.
One should rebuke them, saying:
"Venerable one! You have lost a great benefit;
when the Prātimokṣa was recited every half-month, you did not show respect, you were not single-minded in mindfulness, and you did not listen to the Dharma with attentive ears."
Having rebuked her thus, it is a *pāyattika*.

The sixty matters are concluded. "If a bhikṣuṇī, while in a common dining place, goes to another house before or after a meal without having informed another bhikṣuṇī, except at the time of [distributing] robes, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters the palace of a consecrated Kṣatriya king when the queen’s precious goods have not yet been stored away, even if she merely crosses the threshold, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī makes a needle case from bone, ivory, or horn, having broken it [after its use], it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī makes bed legs, they should be made according to the prescribed measure: eight fingers of the Sugata’s span in length, excluding the part inserted into the frame.”
If she exceeds [the limit], it must be cut off,
and there is a pāyattika. "If a bhikṣuṇī sits or lies upon a mattress stuffed with tūla-cotton,
once she has risen from it, there is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣuṇī makes a *niṣīdana*, she should make it according to the prescribed measure: two *vitasti* of the Sugata in length and one and a half *vitasti* in width, with an additional *vitasti* for the border."
If it exceeds [the prescribed measure], having cut it down, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes a wound-covering robe, she should make it according to the proper measure: four sugata-span hands in length and two and a half span hands in width."
If it exceeds [the prescribed measure], it must be cut down, and there is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes a robe imitating the size of the Tathāgata’s robes, and if it exceeds that measure, it must be cut down, and there is a pāyattika offense."
The measurement of the Tathāgata’s robe is nine Sugata-spans in length and six spans in width.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, slanders another with a groundless saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that an object intended for the Saṃgha is diverted to an individual, [does so], it is a pāyattika.
The seventy matters are concluded. "If a bhikṣuṇī wears another's robe without informing the owner, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī gives a robe with her own hands to a layperson or a śramaṇa of another sect, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes an antarvāsa, it should be made according to measure: four Sugata-spans in length and two spans in width."
If she makes it exceeding [the measure], having cut it down, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes a saṃkakṣikā, it should be made according to the standard measure: four sugata-spans in length and two spans in width."
If she makes it exceeding these measurements, having cut it down [to size], it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes a rain-bath robe, she should make it according to the prescribed measure: four Sugata-spaṣṭahastas in length and two spaṣṭahastas in width."
If she exceeds [the prescribed measure] and cuts it down, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī goes to a family that is unable to provide clothing and begs for a kaṭhina robe on behalf of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, does not keep the robes she has received with her person, it is a pāyattika.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having obtained *khādaniya* food or *bhojaniya* food, cooks it again or causes it to be cooked; roasts it again or causes it to be roasted; or fries it again or causes it to be fried, and a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill eats it, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī provides water or a fan while a bhikṣu is eating, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī eats garlic, it is a pāyattika.”
The eighty rules are concluded: "If a bhikṣuṇī accepts food with her own hands from a layperson or a non-Buddhist, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes a living as a physician, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī teaches medical arts to laypeople or to followers of external paths, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī performs work for a layperson, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing she is entering a household where food is being served, enters without first announcing her presence, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī dwells in close association with laypeople or non-Buddhists—whether for the duration of a day or for a mere moment—even down to a park-attendant or a śrāmaṇera, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī swears an oath against another, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī strikes herself and weeps with tears, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
'Noble lady (āryā),
let us go together to such-and-such a house.'"
If she subsequently, out of intolerance toward a certain bhikṣuṇī, reviles her without cause and without having heard the matter with careful discernment, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind of stinginess and envy, guards a family [as her own], it is a pāyattika.
The ninety matters are concluded: "If a bhikṣuṇī reviles a bhikṣu face-to-face, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a disciple who has not yet reached twelve years of seniority, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī who has completed twelve years of rain-retreats keeps a disciple without being endowed with the ten qualities, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī who is endowed with the ten qualities keeps a disciple without performing the formal act of *karmavācanā*, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another has violated the precepts, takes the door-bolt, opens the door of that person's room, and stays there with a man, yet confers full ordination upon him, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a girl less than twenty years of age, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a girl who is twenty years of age without having her undergo the training in the precepts, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon one who has received the training rules but has not completed the training, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, though having completed the training rules, confers full ordination without performing the formal ritual (karmavācanā), it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī gives full ordination to a married woman who has been married for less than twelve years, it is a pāyattika.
[The hundred rules are concluded. "If a bhikṣuṇī gives full ordination to a married woman who has been married for exactly twelve years, but who has not trained in the precepts, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a woman who was previously married and has received the training rules, yet has not completed the training, it is a pāyattika.

Thus he asks three times: "Venerable sirs!
There is purity herein, for you are silent; thus shall this matter be held."
“Venerable sirs! These are the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma), which are recited every half-month during the Prātimokṣa:
‘One should train oneself to wear the inner robe neatly.’”
"One should train oneself to wear the outer robe neatly.
One should train oneself to enter a house while properly covering the body.
One should train oneself to enter a house while looking attentively."
"One should train oneself: 'One shall enter a house with a low voice.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not enter a house laughing.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not enter a house with the head covered.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house with my robe tucked up over one shoulder.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house walking on my toes.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house with hands on hips.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house swaying the body.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house shaking the head.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house swinging the arms.'"
"One should train oneself to sit within a house with the body well-covered.
One should train oneself to sit within a house while looking attentively.
One should train oneself to sit within a house with a low voice."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit inside a house laughing.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit inside a house with my head covered.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit inside a house with my robe tucked over one shoulder.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit inside a house with my knees tucked up.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit inside a house with my legs crossed.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit inside a house with my hands on my hips.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Remaining seated within the house without moving the hands or feet.
One should train oneself: 'Receiving food with a single-minded focus.
One should train oneself: 'Eating soup and rice in equal measure.'"
"One should train oneself not to eat by scooping out half the food.
One should train oneself not to eat by stuffing the cheeks.
One should train oneself not to eat by sticking out the tongue."
"One should train oneself not to take large mouthfuls of food.
One should train oneself not to open one's mouth while waiting for food.
One should train oneself not to pick at the food with the mouth."
"One should train oneself not to bite off half a morsel of food.
One should train oneself not to speak with food in one's mouth.
One should train oneself not to wipe the bowl with the fingers while eating."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not eat while licking my hands.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not eat while licking my fingers.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not eat while making smacking sounds.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not eat by inhaling.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not swallow food whole.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not let food fall.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One shall not eat with the hand raised.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not look at the bowl of a fellow practitioner with a mind of disdain while eating.
One should train oneself: 'One shall look at one's own bowl with a composed mind while eating.'"
"One should train oneself: 'When not ill, one shall not seek food for oneself.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not cover the soup with rice in hopes of obtaining more.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not receive a drinking vessel with greasy hands.'"
"One should train oneself not to discard leftover food from one's bowl on the ground.
One should train oneself not to stand and preach the Dharma to a person who is seated, except when one is ill."
"One should train oneself: unless one is ill, one shall not preach the Dharma while seated to someone who is lying down.
One should train oneself: unless one is ill, one shall not preach the Dharma while sitting on a lower seat to someone on a high bed."
"One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to one wearing leather sandals.
One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to one wearing wooden clogs.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who has their head covered, except in cases of illness.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who has their head wrapped, except in cases of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who is squatting with knees drawn up, except when ill.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who is sitting with legs crossed over the knees, except when ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to one who is carrying a sword.
One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to one who is holding a bow and arrows.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one holding a staff, except when they are ill.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one holding a parasol, except when they are ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except when ill, I shall not teach the Dharma to someone who is behind while I am in front.
One should train oneself: 'Except when ill, I shall not teach the Dharma to someone who is riding a mount.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except in cases of illness, one shall not teach the Dharma to those outside the path while remaining within the path.
One should train oneself: 'Except in cases of illness, one shall not stand while defecating or urinating.'"
"One should not climb a tree higher than a person, except for a great reason;
this is how one should train. Venerable sirs!
The rules of training for the community have been recited."
"Now I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this matter?
Thus he asks three times: "Venerable ones!"
"In this matter, we are pure because we remain silent; thus shall this matter be upheld.
"Venerable sirs! These are the seven principles for the settlement of disputes."
Every half-month, the Prātimokṣa is recited.

"If, according to the matter and in accordance with the person, one should grant the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence) to a person for whom it is appropriate, then one should grant the *saṃmukha-vinaya*."
"To one who should be granted the *smṛtivinaya*, grant the *smṛtivinaya*.
To one who should be granted the *amūḍhavinaya*, grant the *amūḍhavinaya*."
"To those who should be dealt with through their own confession, one should grant the *pātimokkha* procedure of confession (*sāmukkaṃsika*);
to those whose offense should be sought, one should grant the *pātimokkha* procedure of seeking the offense (*tassapāpiyasika*)."
"To one who should be granted the *tassapāpiyasika* (further-punishment) discipline, grant the *tassapāpiyasika* discipline.
To one who should be granted the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering-over-as-with-grass) discipline, grant the *tiṇavatthāraka* discipline."
"Venerable sirs! The seven methods for settling disputes have been explained.
Now I ask the venerable sirs: [Is this clear?]"
"Is there purity herein?
Thus he asks three times: "Venerable sirs!
Since there is silence, you are pure herein; thus shall this matter be upheld."

"Venerable sisters! The introduction to the precepts has been recited; the eight *pārājika* rules have been recited; the nineteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules have been recited; the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules have been recited; the one hundred and forty-one *pāyattika* rules have been recited; the eight *prātideśanīya* rules have been recited; the rules of training (*śaikṣadharma*) have been recited; the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*) have been recited; and the rules of conformity (*anudharmika*) have been recited. These are called the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—the Dharma of the bhikṣuṇīs—which has entered into the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra*. This Dharma is the Dharma that accords with the Dharma; all of you should train yourselves and not transgress it."
"Thus [he spoke]."
